v1, CARRYING CAPACITY: the sixth song, a skeleton (the whole shape, played bare). You said "make it unique"; this is what I took that to mean, and it is yours to overrule.
THE IDEA: I did not write a riff. The song has one rule and one dial. The rule is the oldest model of a population (next year's number is this year's, times how fast it breeds, times the room left). It is worked out once every half bar, and the number it gives IS that half bar: how many of its six places the band strikes, where the accent falls, how high the accent is. The form is only the dial being turned up and brought back down:
- 0:00 it grows from nothing to a plain shuffle, and stays there: the same half bar every time (0:14);
- 0:28 it splits: two half bars that take turns; 0:42 four; 0:56 eight (the riff doubles its own length);
- 1:10 it stops repeating altogether, and is still plainly the same riff;
- 1:27 it LOCKS, by itself, on a cycle five half bars long; 1:58 on three; 2:14 on six. Nobody chose five or three: they are in the rule. Against a bar of two they are this record's odd meters, found and not written;
- 2:24 the dial is at the top: it screams, then there is nothing at all for a bar or more (after its highest number the rule always gives its lowest), and a long low boom falls through the hole; then it climbs back;
- 2:52 the dial comes down through four, two, one, and at 3:13 the song dies out on three single notes.
HOW IT IS UNLIKE THE OTHER FIVE: it is in triplets (the others are in straight sixteenths) and faster (138; they are 100 to 126); on E (they sit on F and C); its drums are a DRUM MACHINE, new on this record; and the tune on top is not written in the song at all. That track holds only the rule, and the engine works the notes out itself (a feature no song here had used); I checked its 171 notes against mine and none differ.

Running Total is parked out of the draw until you have heard it: it was offered three times running.)
There are two things a band can do with a cycle that does not fit the bar. It can hold the bar and let the cycle turn against it: that is the lock on three (2:01), where the snare stays on the bar's third beat and the riff comes round under it. Or it can drop the bar and go with the cycle. Until now both locks did the first. Now the lock on five (1:27) does the second: for its seventeen seconds the song is IN five.
The cycle is ten beats long, and the machine counts it the way a drummer counts ten: four, four and two. The snare is on the third beat of each four (the first of them lands on the cycle's one lonely low note), both beats of the two are snare, a push, and the cymbal is on the head of each cycle. Nothing marks the song's own bar there but the hat, which never stops. After four times round, ten bars have gone by, and the bar and the cycle meet again at 1:44, where the wall comes back.

v6, FOUR KEYS, ONE SCALE (a whole-song round on Carrying Capacity. The draw gave False Summit, a whole-song round: I read it whole an hour ago for its v13 and have nothing new, so I passed and took this, on an idea with a reason in the song.)
Until now this song never left E: three and a half minutes on one low string, every stretch told apart by rhythm alone. The scale it is written in has a property an ordinary scale does not: moved up a minor third it is THE SAME EIGHT NOTES. So the band can change key without changing a note of its scale, and four such steps come back to where they started: E, G, B flat, D flat, E. The song now takes that road, one step at each change of state:
- 1:27, where the riff locks on five: everything a minor third up, on G. The wall at 1:44 stays there.
- 2:01, where it locks on three (on the cymbal): on B flat, the far side of the circle from E.
- 2:24, the top of the dial: on D flat. The guitars' screams are now the highest notes in the song. The bass does not go up with them: it goes UNDER, to the D flat below its E, the lowest note it plays anywhere.
- 2:52, the dial comes down: E. For the guitars it is a fall of a sixth back onto the open string. For the bass it is one more minor third UP, from that low D flat to the E it began on: four steps up, and home.
It is this record's subject again, in pitch this time: a long cycle that lines up. The tune and the chips move with the band (the engine works the tune out from the same ladder, moved; I checked its 183 notes against mine and none differ). The machine's kick and its boom stay on E, which is in the scale in all four keys.
